# Stabbed at the Front 

After 1918 the myth was created that the German army only lost the war because it had been ‘stabbed in the back’ by defeatists and revolutionaries on the Home Front. Alexander Watson reviews the clear evidence that in reality it simply lost the will to go on fighting.

 Alexander Watson | Published in History Today Volume 58 Issue 11 November 2008 

To generations familiar with the total defeat of Hitler’s Reich in 1945, the Allied victory over the Germans in the First World War appears curiously incomplete. When the armistice came into force on November 11th, 1918, the German Field Army in the west numbered 2,500,000 and was still in position mainly on foreign soil. Between the wars, right-wing advocates of the ‘stab in the back’ legend seized on these facts to argue that Germany had remained undefeated in the field, putting the blame instead on the outbreak of revolution at home in early November for the humiliating capitulation.

Yet the fact is that on September 29th, a full month before the beginning of the unrest at home, Germany’s military leaders, General Erich Ludendorff and Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg, had urgently demanded that an immediate armistice be organized. Their desperate desire for peace derived not from any domestic considerations nor even the weakness of Germany’s allies; it was due principally to the parlous state of their army. The war had been above all a contest of endurance and, during the course of 1918, the accumulated strain and the hopelessness of its situation had broken the army’s will to continue fighting. A psychological crisis, experienced first by the fighting soldiers and their officers but then spreading up through the ranks to the top levels of the High Command, caused a disastrous deterioration in combat motivation and fighting efficiency, ultimately forcing Germany’s ignominious exit from the war.

The year 1918 had begun promisingly for the Germans. The army had suffered 1,500,000 killed by the end of 1917 and was displaying ominous signs of war weariness, most visible in the rising incidence of desertion and a spate of small-scale mutinies in the second half of the year; but its prospects had been considerably improved by the outbreak of the October Revolution in Russia. The Bolsheviks’ rapid withdrawal from the war allowed Ludendorff to plan a major ‘last card’ offensive in the west, designed to administer a knockout blow before the US army mustered in overwhelming strength in Europe. By transferring troops from eastern theatres over the winter of 1917-18, the Germans were able to concentrate 191 divisions in the west against the 178 of the Allies. The youngest and fittest men were assembled in the 56 divisions earmarked to lead the offensive and they were given special assault training and the best equipment. These thorough preparations, combined with the fact that Russia was now out of the war, raised German morale considerably. Yet the soldiers’ newfound optimism was fragile and based on the assumption that the coming offensive would swiftly achieve a decisive victory, enabling them finally to return home. One infantry officer, Lieutenant Friedrich Müller, expressed the dominant mood when he pleaded in his diary just before the offensive: ‘God, give us Germans victory, don’t place the people under still greater tests.’

When the great assault began on the morning of March 21st, 1918, against British lines guarding the Somme, it was initially devastating. A five-hour preparatory bombardment, in which 1,160,000 shells were fired into the positions of the British Fifth and Third Armies, was followed by infantry attacks in thick fog. German troops rapidly overran British forward defences and moved through into the fortified areas behind. Although the ambitious objectives set for the first day were not reached, the Germans did capture almost 100 square miles of ground and 500 guns and inflicted over 38,000 casualties. The following days saw more German gains, but as resistance stiffened and the infantry units outran their artillery support and supply lines, the advance slowed. When it finally came to a halt on April 5th, the army had penetrated 40 miles behind Allied lines, causing 212,000 casualties, but it had failed to create a decisive breakthrough. Subsequent attacks launched in Flanders (April 9th to 11th), against Amiens (April 24th), on the River Aisne (May 27th) and Matz (June 9th), and, finally, at Rheims (July 15th) inflicted hundreds of thousands more losses on the British and French armies, but pushed back rather than ruptured the Allied lines, creating enormous, indefensible salients. The cost of these efforts for the Germans was prohibitive: total losses during the offensive amounted to some 978,000 men. Moreover, whereas the Allies were able to replace their casualties with the fresh American troops arriving in France, the Germans had no adequate reserves. By mid-July, the Germans found themselves holding a weakly fortified front seventy-five miles longer than in March, but with their strength reduced to 3,580,000 men. Infantry companies, once 120 strong, now typically had just seventy to ninety soldiers.

The heavy casualties and failure to win a quick, decisive victory seriously affected the morale and the resilience of the German army. Junior officers and the well-trained men of the élite divisions that had spearheaded the assaults suffered disproportionately severe losses. The trenches were now largely held by inferior units made up of older, unenthusiastic and less well-equipped men. Even as early as the end of April, despondency was widespread and troops had become noticeably more hesitant in attack. Discipline suffered under the immense physical strain and hunger, a perennial problem for the German army due to the food shortages caused by the British naval blockade, became severely disruptive. During the spring, underfed combatants delayed the advance by stopping to plunder well-stocked French towns and Allied depots for food and alcohol. When attacks began to fail and opportunities for such looting declined, hungry soldiers, sometimes led by their NCOs and officers, stole their own army’s provisions. In May at least one division was forced to equip its supply trains with light machine-guns to ward off pillagers. Exhaustion was also beginning to affect performance. In May, for example, Infantry Regiment 74 mutinied when ordered to return to the front after previously suffering heavy casualties and ration carriers serving in Infantry Regiment 97 refused to go up the line. The following month, Infantry Regiment 419 faced both mutiny and desertions. By the middle of June, the Second Army command on the Somme was complaining that ‘cases of soldiers openly refusing to obey orders are increasing to an alarming extent’.

Deteriorating discipline at the front in the early summer was matched at the same time by even more serious insubordination along the army’s lines of communication. In May, transports transferring middle-aged reservists from the Eastern Front regularly arrived in France and Flanders lacking up to twenty per cent of their proper complement. Desertion and even worse forms of dissent soon spread to drafts travelling directly from Germany. Troops delayed their departure by refusing to embark, by rioting and by vandalising stations. Once underway, they activated their trains’ emergency brakes and, during halts, uncoupled their wagons from the locomotive. Officers were assaulted and, in one especially serious incident, a draft of 500 soldiers opened fire on a railway platform and eighty of them deserted. Ludendorff later suggested that young recruits had been radicalized in Germany, poisoning the army with the home front’s treachery. The presence among them of disaffected ex-munitions workers, conscripted as punishment for striking, and old, often unfit soldiers dredged from sedentary occupations for service at the front cannot have helped. Yet, given that morale in home training units had in fact been reasonably good until quite late in the war, it seems more likely that veterans – soldiers who had already served on the Eastern Front, ex-prisoners of war from Russia and wounded soldiers from Ludendorff’s supposedly loyal Field Army returning reluctantly from hospital to the front – were the ringleaders in these disturbances.

Vulnerably positioned, starved of manpower, demoralized and by this time also in the grip of an influenza epidemic, the German army was ill-prepared to repel the sudden and ferocious counter-attack launched by the French, British and Americans at the Marne on July 18th. The initial surprise assault, spearheaded by massed tank formations and supported by over 2,000 guns, advanced up to five miles and captured 12,000 prisoners, stopping the Germans’ own Rheims offensive and decisively returning the initiative to the Allies. Strategically, as the Army Group Commander, Crown Prince Rupprecht, recognized, it was ‘a turning point of the war’. Ludendorff, too, was shaken, but at first reluctant to concede that the German army must now stand on the defensive. This realization, however, was forced on him by the success of the Allies’ next major attack outside Amiens on August 8th, where his Second Army was surprised by the British Fourth and French First Armies, supported by 3,700 guns and more than 500 tanks. In this attack, the Allies advanced up to eight miles and captured 18,000 prisoners in what Ludendorff later famously described as ‘the black day of the German army in the history of this war’. Particularly disturbing was not merely the scale of defeat, but the low morale evinced by the troops which had made it possible. Ludendorff wrote:

> I was told of behaviour which, I openly confess, I should not have thought possible in the German army; whole bodies of our men had surrendered to single troopers, or isolated squadrons. Retiring troops, meeting a fresh division going bravely into action, had shouted out things like ‘Blackleg’, and ‘You’re prolonging the war’.

As he confided to one of his staff officers in the aftermath of the disaster, ‘our troops are more or less finished’.

This judgement was amply confirmed throughout the second half of August and September as the Allies directed rolling attacks against different points of the German line. Faced with a well-trained enemy bolstered by enormous reserves of American manpower, abundant munitions, air superiority and a tank force against which they had no effective counter-measure, the morale of Ludendorff’s soldiers deteriorated still further. According to the postal censor of the German Fifth Army, fighting in the Argonne region, troops’ letters at the end of August were characterized by a ‘widespread war weariness, moroseness and depression’. By early September, soldiers of the Sixth Army further north had ‘come to terms [in their correspondence] with what for them is the plain fact: “We cannot win” and in some cases even add to this the view that Germany will inevitably be defeated’. The heavy fighting during these two months cost the Germans well over 400,000 casualties and, exacerbated by Ludendorff’s reluctance to retreat to a shorter defensive line, eroded the reserve of fresh divisions at the High Command’s disposal. Badly depleted, worn-out units were forced to remain in action for unprecedentedly long periods. According to one military psychiatrist, the army was driven to a severe condition of ‘neurasthenic exhaustion’. Crown Prince Rupprecht recorded how, in early September, one overstrained battalion had fled at the cry, ‘the English are coming’. At the end of the month, the commander of Third Army, Lieutenant General von Einem, similarly noted with disgust how a whole division had run when attacked.
